utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Very good morning to everybody. May we please hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the enlarged appearances for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Nicholas Koumjian, Kapila Waidyaratne, and Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic, John Ostojic, and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before starting, I have to express my gratitude that already today, the registry has provided us with a list of the documents of yesterday. No doubt that during this marathon, there was a slight mistake, but we can rely on this List 6 of the new documents. I hope you all have it with you, and it ends with S276A, Official Gazette Number 1. Not to forget, having now Official Gazette Number 1, this makes greedy [phoen] in the direction. What about the last Official Gazette before this Official Gazette Number 1? Remember, we discussed the issue whether or not there was a change of the board of editors in Kozarski Vjesnik, and I think it's of some interest whether or not there was a change or some continuity in the Official Gazettes in Prijedor. And therefore, I would invite the OTP to go through their own documents, whether or not they have available the last former Official Gazette before this one, Number 1, from May 1992. We have to come back to some of these documents during the hearing of Madam Tabeau and Mr. Inayat. Having had a look on the issues already at stake as regards Mr. Inayat, I would ask the parties whether or not it could be possible that the parties have, first of all, a meeting with Mr. Inayat for a first clarification of formalities of the core issues and the central issues which are really relevant for this case - they have, no doubt, to be discussed in the courtroom. But that we can already exclude the first layer of more or less formal problems in this informal setting. And I would appreciate if the parties could agree on this procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's acceptable, Your Honour, to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm not prepared yet to do that, but I think it could set a precedent of having our witnesses preinterviewed that we do not want to see established. Unless the Defence will allow me to interview all their witnesses before they testify. It's the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't think it's now -- it's not a question of interviewing a witness; it's a question of clarification how some documents were found or not. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would propose alternatively that I could get together with the Defence if there's questions about our procedures, and I can give them information that they may request regarding this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sometimes the Judges should have also advantages from this party system, and therefore I invite the parties to find out the best way how to proceed in the way that we can really concentrate on the core issues that we can call issues worthwhile discussing in the courtroom, because no doubt to a certain extent Mr. Inayat is part of one of the parties in this case. So let's -- if there are no other administrative matters, I can't see them. Then we -- Mr. Koumjian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry, just to remind Your Honour, we do have -- Your Honours requested to view originals of some of the documents. Provisional S254, S258, S264, which was a Kozarski Vjesnik I believe. Is this the one the Court asked for better copies? Those copies are available, and the original can be viewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May it please be presented first to the Defence, and then to the Bench. Okay, let's start with the copy of S264. Can we all agree that this is readable, and therefore a copy to work with of Kozarski Vjesnik of 25 September, 1992, S264B.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can accept that this is the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, we have seen for the transcript the original Radno Izdenje of Kozarski Vjesnik of 25 September, 1992, page 2 in front of us, and we have seen that this is a real copy. Thank you for this. This problem has been solved. Thank you. Then let's turn to Document S258. Are there any comments by the OTP as regards to this combination of two sheets of paper?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Apparently they were attached when found. The faxed document or the sheet showing the fax number is not -- at this point we don't see any particular -- it's not of particular interest to us. But it was attached to the other document. It may have some information regarding how that document was received at the location where it was seized.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Probably there remains a question for Mr. Inayat, some problems from the side of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Hopefully we'll be able to clarify that matter with Mr. Inayat, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But we have seen and clarified that indeed there were two sheets of papers, and therefore having seen the documents, these documents are admitted into evidence as S258A-1, the stripe with fax coordinates, and the attached document, -2. The original may be returned to the OTP. Then S254, I can see by the red registration number that indeed evidently you didn't get a better copy. Or this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's the original that we seized, or that's the document we seized.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The document seized. And I think it was already admitted into evidence. Please correct me, Madam Registrar, if not. It was admitted. Here it remains only to have at least an attempt to translate the content of the stamp that we find at the bottom of this document. The document may be returned to the OTP. Thank you. So if we can rely on the list before us, it remains only to be shown the original of S267, and not yet admitted was S273. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe some of those documents have already been submitted for analysis, and they are out of the building. So that may take some time. They are not available for a period of time. We'll check on that, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: They should be available in due time before we hear Mr. Inayat in the courtroom once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That may require taking them away from the document examiners, and we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's find a solution in the moment we have fixed the date for the hearing of Mr. Inayat. So anything else to be discussed urgently this morning? Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I do have one issue that was raised by the Court yesterday towards the conclusion of our session. And it was I think an interesting and important matter which perhaps we can address this morning. The Court seemed to suggest that various witnesses should be compelled to call, either by the Office of the Prosecution, the Defence, or by the Court as permitted by the rules. Although we do not want and do not intend to infringe upon the rights of other defendants in this case, such as Mr. Mrdja, General Talic, or Mr. Brdjanin, we do believe that there was one particular witness that might be helpful to us that the Office of the Prosecutor has interviewed who is a defendant who was represented during the interview process. The issues relating to Dr. Biljana Plavsic we believe may be relevant to this case if indeed the Office of the Prosecutor intends to continue with their allegations and assertions based upon joint action and concert with criminal activity. With respect to the subcategories of all those issues, we believe that Dr. Plavsic voluntarily, based upon information believed while being represented by counsel, has given extensive interviews to the OTP on these and other matters. By way of background, the Court may already know that Dr. Plavsic was one of five members of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, in particular, during the relevant time periods in this case. Although we don't know the sum and substance of that interview or the matters in which she responded to, we believe that it may be of assistance to both the Court and the Defence in establishing some of these preliminary yet fundamental issues. So we would ask orally and, if necessary, in writing that the OTP provide and produce that interview and those documents to us at a reasonable time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can understand your contribution. Nevertheless, you will understand that the notion "may be of assistance" seems not to be enough. It should be more concrete as to what points Dr. Plavsic may and really can assist us in finding the truth and justice in this case. And therefore, it would indeed be helpful for the evaluation and the decision on this issue if the Defence could provide us with a document or in writing what they expect to hear from Dr. Plavsic and, in addition, the relevance for this case inconcreto for what charges, in relation to what facts. And then no doubt, we have to decide whether to ask the OTP or whether to act ex officio. If not, the OTP plans ex officio to call Dr. Plavsic in this case. And it still remains open, and I want to ask the representative of the OTP: When will the Defence counsel of Mr. Mrdja arrive in The Hague in order to find out whether or not it is possible, necessary, mandatory, to hear Mr. Mrdja in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, I can tell the Court informally, because again I did speak to him but I don't represent him by any means, that he told me he was trying to arrange with the registry to come next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I just want to make it clear that our position in the OTP is we decide which witnesses we're going to call on our case. If the Defence wants to call witnesses, they can call witness in their case. But I think the rules envision that the choice of witnesses by the OTP is our choice. The Court also has the power to call witnesses on its own, and the Defence does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt about this. But please understand that we don't want to interfere in the one or other party's case, and the first right to call a witness during a case is for the party. And only if we know definitively that a party will not hear a witness, then it's up to us to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I can state definitively that the OTP will not be calling any person who are accused as witnesses in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the same is true for persons already convicted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On this particular case, that is true. Your Honour may recall we did attempt to call one person who was convicted on this case earlier, and there may be circumstances --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. But if I recall correctly, it was another municipality, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And I have persons in mind closer to this case already convicted, and I'm more than surprised not to have presented these persons. I don't know why, but -- I can't imagine. Anything else to discuss today?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So we can turn to the already-waiting witness. May I ask, anything changed? What about the actual protective measures necessary for Witness 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there are no protective measures requested by this witness. He has testified in previous trials in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So we can ask the usher to bring in Mr. Jusuf Arifagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Jusuf Arifagic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Arifagic. You can hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please hear your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, be seated and be open to answer the questions of the OTP. The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, could you kindly state your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: 17th of August, 1961.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You were born in Kozarac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your father's name is Dervis Arifagic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You have a brother and a sister?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Both of them are married?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was your education? Where did you have your primary education?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I completed my primary education in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And your secondary education, did you go to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I completed my secondary education at the technical school in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you specialise in any particular field?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Upon the completion of the secondary technical school, I became a machine technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Arifagic, before we proceed further, you said that you had a brother -- you have a brother. Can I know the name of this brother, please, of the brother?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: My brother's name is Adem, Adem Arifagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And the sister's name?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Emira Causagic. She is married.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, after your secondary education, did you do your compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did my compulsory military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: If I say that it was in the year 1980 and 1981, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where did you serve?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I did my military service in Pancevo near Belgrade, and only a small part of it in Belgrade itself, in these two cities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: That was in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was it a special unit, or did you have any specialised training during this service?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the infantry. My unit was a special unit. It was a sabotage unit of the general headquarters of the then Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: After your compulsory service, did you serve with the reserve?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, after your service, military service, were you engaged in any kind of employment?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I found employment in Croatia. I worked in a Croatian company as a foreman, and I was involved in -- I worked with anti-corrosive agents and anti-corrosive protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, after you served in Croatia, you continued to work in the same field, and you worked in Libya, am I correct, for almost -- for five and a half years?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: In between this period, you used to come to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Kozarac for holidays every four or five months.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And you lived with the parents. And in the year 1986, you got married?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: By that marriage, you had a child. And --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had a daughter in this marriage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And you lived with the parents in the parental house at Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Arifagic, could you explain why you returned to Kozarac in 1991 and for how long you were there.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: In December of 1991, I went back to Kozarac. My sole reason for going back to Kozarac was my desire to start building a family house of my own. I remained there in December 1991. And in early 1992, I started working on my family house. And sometime in March, that is, prior to the outbreak of the conflict, I moved into this house with my family. So that was the reason why I went back and why I took a longer leave, that is, to complete my house and to move in with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in the period -- to be specific, in the year of 1991 and 1992, were you involved in politics while you were in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You were not a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you, if I may ask you -- you can refrain from answering, did you vote in the elections, the last election which was held in Kozarac in 1991 and 1992 -- 1990, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, moving to another area, speaking about Kozarac, could you explain as to -- about Kozarac, which villages, what ethnicity was the population that was in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: The majority of the Kozarac population, 86, 87 per cent, were Bosniak, Muslim, and the remainder of the population, 1 or 2 per cent perhaps Serbs, and another smaller percentage of Croats, Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Kozarac is an area comprised of many villages and hamlets and mainly populated by Muslims. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: These villages, if I name some, were Kamicani, Kevljani, Babici, Hrnici, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, are you aware of the villages which surrounded this area which you call Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were there Serb villages, or mainly consisting of a population of Serbian nationality?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Serbs constituted the majority in these villages except for one village which was predominantly Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Can you name some of these villages that you name as -- or which surrounded Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Vidovici, Balte, Lamovita, Omarska, Jelicka, Maricka, Tomasica, those would be these villages, Jaruge, Orlovci, Donji/Gornji Garevci.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I will take your attention to another area which will be towards the year 1992, the beginning of 1992. In January, you were in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you notice or observe any change that took -- that happened during that time relating to the takeover in April? If I specifically say, any military changes or politically changes that you observed.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: What I was able to observe concerned the military situation. Up until that time, this was not very usual; however, from January 1992, one could observe intense movements of the military columns and vehicles of the JNA. According to our information, the JNA when withdrawing from Croatia stationed a number of their units in the surroundings of Prijedor and Kozarac. Very often, one could see convoys of vehicles passing on the road from Prijedor to Banja Luka. Some of these convoys passed through Kozarac and to quarters near Benkovac not far from the Mrakovica monument. Every day one could see in the streets of Kozarac local Serbs or Serbs from the surrounding villages walking around the streets with weapons after they had come back from the front line near Lipik. Very often in those days they carried weapons, even when they were in cafes. The population of Kozarac got irritated as a result of that because they were very often quite aggressive would open fire, shoot in the air, or throw hand grenades. So these were the things that were not normal or customary prior to that period of time in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Going further, did you observe the arming of people, specifically the Serbs in that area?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: We did. Most of the Serbs from the area were armed ever since 1991. According to the knowledge we had, in the 5th Kozarac Brigade, that is, the Prijedor brigade, there were many of them who participated in operations in Croatia. So when they came back from the theater, they kept their weapons with them while they were on leave. This caused irritation amongst the citizens of Kozarac. Very often during the night, one could hear shooting, and this influenced the overall situation and the sense of insecurity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: The association or the contacts between the Serb population and the Muslim population during this time, did you observe a change in that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Well, this affected the way they communicated and behaved. Very often, they would accuse us of being deserters and they said that it would be perfectly normal for us to participate alongside them in the war of Croatia with the aim of preserving Yugoslavia. They argued that they wanted to preserve Yugoslavia, and they often referred to us Muslims as Ustashas, as deserters, as betrayers of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: During this time, Mr. Arifagic, what developments or change did you see in the TV and the radio, in the programmes that you watched?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Sometime in late February, I noticed that the programme which we normally followed up until that period of time, that is, the Bosnian TV, the Sarajevo TV - we did have opportunity to watch Croatian programmes also - disappeared all of a sudden. All these programmes could no longer be seen, and we could follow only broadcasts from Banja Luka and Belgrade. The explanation was that the JNA had taken over the TV relay at the Kozara mountain, and that allegedly everything was now under control. They also said that some kind of Banja Luka SAO Krajina had been established, so we could watch from then on the Banja Luka and Belgrade TV. This also included the Prijedor TV and radio stations. They started broadcasting programmes which were not usual until that time. All of a sudden, we started listening to the songs which ten years ago would have been forbidden. There would have been a ban on broadcasting such songs. And there were interviews, for instance, with the leaders of the SDS party. And most of these interviews boiled down to the desire to preserve Yugoslavia, that there was a constitutional right for them to preserve Yugoslavia, and that Muslims and Croats and Ustashas wanted to destroy Yugoslavia and similar allegations were broadcast at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, you referred to in your answer saying that there were discussions by political leaders of the SDS. Do you recall any specific -- any special person or leader from those parties -- from the party of SDS who came on TV or radio?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: As I have already indicated, I was not involved in politics, so I didn't know most of these leaders. However, the majority of them were members of the SDS leadership in Banja Luka, perhaps a small number of them were in Prijedor. We knew that they were leaders of the SDS, local leaders of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Going a step further, in February, month of February 1992, did you observe helicopters moving in the area of Kozarac and the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, during that period of time, one could observe intense movements of helicopters. They flew in the airspace of the Kozara region, over Kozara mountain. I remember I once was able to see a helicopter land in a nearby Serb village, the village of Balte.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you learn as to why these helicopters were moving around that area and why it landed in Balte? Did you pursue that matter?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: According to our sources, this helicopter landed in Balte with cargos of weapons, that there was an arming of the local population going on in this village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Local population means they were Serbs? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, the village of Balte was in the border of Kozarac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And how would you define that village? Was it a Serb majority that lived there, or Muslims population, non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: The village of Balte was exclusively populated by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May I be permitted to, Your Honour, use S14, the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so, with the assistance of the usher. I don't want to be impolite, but as we have heard a lot of these issues already beforehand with the assistance of other witnesses, could you please be so kind and concentrate on the core issues where we decided that it would be necessary to hear this witness in addition, giving some additional information, and go more concretely into details and not leave it to answers such as "according to our sources" and not asking what are these sources. And then the answer "local population means they were Serbs" and leave it with the answer "yes." I don't think it helps very much. I would ask you to go more into details. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I would do my best, Your Honour. I will follow your advice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, would you kindly indicate to the Court as to the place that you referred to as Balte, the village of Balte. If the audiovisual person could -- you could look at the map and first point out to the place where you referred to as the village of Balte. The place that you are pointing out, it is in the borders of --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, Balte is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How far was the village of Balte from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: The village of Balte is perhaps 1 kilometre, to 1 kilometre and a half, away from my village, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Did we discuss the hamlet of G. Balte or D. Balte?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I will come to that, Your Honour. My next question is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in the map it is indicated as G. Balte. Is it Gornji Balte?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. I thank the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: It is true there is Gornji Balte and Donja Balte. But actually it is a very small village and represents a whole. The two hamlets represent the whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What does Gornji and Donja Balte mean?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Gornji Balte is the upper Balte. They are situated a little bit further up with respect to Kozarac, whereas Donja Balte is situated towards Kamicani, in the lower area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you also take this opportunity, and you spoke about a place called Benkovac. If the map... If it could be moved?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And also could you point out the place Mrakovica.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How far was Mrakovica from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And also, taking this opportunity, could you also show the village of Javori, if the map... Is that shown in that map?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I don't think it is. I cannot find the name of the village of Javori here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was it -- how far was it from Kozarac? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: From the centre of Kozarac, maybe 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, we were -- thank you. We were talking about the village of Balte and its population, and you said that it was mainly consisting of the Serb -- a Serb population there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And you, in your previous answer, when you were referring to the distribution of weapons or the Serbs receiving weapons, you said "our resources" or - sorry - "our sources." Could you explain how you heard or got to know about this, what your source was?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I think that on one occasion, even the Kozarac police received the information that a helicopter had landed in the village of Balte, that weapons were being brought in, and they tried to carry out an investigation. However, they were prevented from doing so, and they came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who told you this?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: A cousin of mine who worked in the police in Kozarac. I think he was a member of the patrol who went there. Later, we talked, and he told me that there was an arming of the population going on from the village of Balte and the surrounding villages, that they had information to that effect, that they had tried to enter the village but couldn't do so, so they went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Arifagic, you mentioned a person as a cousin of mine who worked in the police. Are you able to give the name of this person?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could we go in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Confirmed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, now, going ahead, did you learn that these Serbs had taken over the power in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: If I say that it was on the 30th of April, 1992, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, after the takeover on the 30th of April, what did you hear and see?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: The explanation we were given is that all the policemen who had up to that point worked at the police station in Prijedor were disarmed and told to leave their jobs, that the SDS took over power in Prijedor. And they convinced all the population of Prijedor Municipality that they had nothing to fear and that they had every reason to feel safe because now everything was going to be all right. The population from the surrounding villages were the predominantly Muslim and Croat population and was required to sign an oath of loyalty to the SDS authorities in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, how did you get to know -- did you hear this -- how did you have this information that the non-Serbs had to sign the loyalty oath?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: It was broadcast on the local radio and TV, mainly the radio, every day, that the local population should sign an oath of loyalty. This was also required from those policemen who had been disarmed. They said if they signed the oath of loyalty to the SDS and the authorities in Prijedor, they can stay and continue to work for the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did they say as to what would happen if they did not do that, what would result or the consequences would be?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Well, mainly those who failed to sign the oath of loyalty were supposed to turn in their weapons, no matter whether legally or illegally owned. Hunting rifles, all kinds of weapons, that's what was requested. And if not, then the JNA would take over control of the area. What that really meant was that there would be an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Arifagic, previously in answer to one of the questions, you said that "the Muslim and Croat population was required to sign an oath of loyalty to the SDS authorities in Prijedor." Did you know any of these people from the authorities in the SDS in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Very few, only what was broadcast on the radio, the names of as I Simo Drljaca, Radmilo Zeljaja, those people mainly. That's what I could hear. The Crisis Staff in Prijedor was also referred to, Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you hear any other names during those announcements, members of the Crisis Staff in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recall any of those, other than the names that you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No, not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, now, what did you do? Did you abide by the request or the announcements or the orders by the SDS in Prijedor? Did you want to sign a loyalty oath?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did the population, the majority in Kozarac, agree to abide by what was announced by the new Serb authorities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: In the sense of signing an oath of loyalty, no, we were not prepared to do that. We were still trying to follow the instructions from the Sarajevo government, and we were in touch with people who had been elected in the last elections to be local representatives of the government at the local level. And we had conversations with them. They wanted our opinion, and the decision by the population of Kozarac was to sign no oath of loyalty. We kept emphasising that we did not want to attack anyone; we just wanted to stay in our homes and live on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you believe -- what did you believe would happen if you did not sign the oath?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: At that moment, we had no idea what could happen. But we did have some information that certain villages did, indeed, sign oaths of loyalty and turn in their weapons, but that despite that, these same villages were later attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you any local representative -- you referred to some people as the local representatives from the locality of Kozarac and other Muslim areas. Did any of these people speak to the authorities in Prijedor, the newly established authorities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were in touch all the time. They talked -- they tried to reach an agreement. They tried to convey the opinion of the citizens of Kozarac, to explain the situation that they had every guarantee from us in Kozarac that we would never attack anyone, that the only thing we wanted was to stay in Kozarac but that we could not sign an oath of loyalty to an authority that was proclaimed and supposed to be in charge of our area too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: In your answer you referred to a situation or -- you used the words: "to explain the situation that they had every guarantee from us in Kozarac that we would not -- never attack anyone." Now, you mean to say "they" in the sense of the authorities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, the authorities in Prijedor. We just wanted to convey very clearly our message and our guarantee that as far as the population of Kozarac was concerned, not a single one of the surrounding Serb villages who we still considered our neighbours would be attacked by us. But we also said that we simply did not want to sign any oath of loyalty to the SDS in Prijedor because we still thought that Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state was in existence. And that the population living in that territory should be loyal and follow the instructions by the government in Sarajevo and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Arifagic, who are the people from the local authorities or from Kozarac who were in touch with the authorities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: If we look at the political situation, it was Becir Medunjanin, Besim Alic, people who were at the head of the SDS [sic] and who had been appointed to official positions in Kozarac local commune at the last elections. When talking about the Kozarac police, then it was the chief of police in Kozarac -- excuse me. When talking about the police, it was the commander of the Kozarac Police Station, Osme, and there was another person who had left the JNA prior to that. Probably he was in disagreement with their war policy and returned to Kozarac. Up to that point, he had been an active officer in the JNA. His name was Sead Cirkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, in your last -- the previous answer, you have -- you said: "People who were at the head of the SDS and who had been appointed to official positions in Kozarac local commune." Isn't it correct that it should be corrected as SDA?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No, what I meant was the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So it should be SDA?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know any persons from the Prijedor authorities, in Prijedor, any persons who were contacted by the Muslims or the authorities in -- people from Kozarac? Who were the people from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I think the commander of the Kozarac Police Station only made contact with the commander of the Prijedor Police Station, Simo Drljaca, I think that was his name. But most often, contact was made with Radmilo Zeljaja as far as I knew. Probably there were other contacts being made with other persons, but I had no opportunity to learn anything about those other contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, before we leave this area, now, who informed you about what was said by the authorities in Prijedor? Were these people that you mentioned, people like Becir Medunjanin and Besim Alic?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, those were the people. After every talk or meeting with the SDS people and after every new information that was obtained, they tried to go out and visit the people on the ground, discuss the newly arisen situation. They wanted local opinion, the opinion of the people of Kozarac. They wanted to know whether they were ready to accept the new conditions and whether they were still not prepared to sign the oath of loyalty. And they wanted to know how to proceed with talks with the authorities in Prijedor, their strategy for these talks very much depended on our response.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you recall that the attack on Kozarac was on the 24th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Before that, the takeover of Prijedor, or the taking of the power in Prijedor was on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So from the 30th of April and the 24th of May, did you take part in any guarding or standing guard at any place?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Since the takeover in Prijedor, we tried to organise ourselves a little -- excuse me. The population of Kozarac wanted to try to control the outer border of Kozarac. We wanted to protect ourselves from any incursions from outside into the Kozarac area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where were you? Where did you stand guard?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I was with a group of people in the Javori, in the village of Javori which had the same population. So it was at the far end of the village of Javori. That was the last village before the village of Balte. We stood guard duty there and tried to prevent anyone from breaking into that area so that nothing unpleasant would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you armed?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: We were mostly armed with hunting rifles. There were people who tried to devise weapons of their own making. Some people had pistols. But mostly, if you had a hunting rifle, then those people who were on duty there tried to control the situation. And when they left, they would just leave their rifle to those who came to relieve them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How many people stood guard there?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: There were perhaps five, six, maybe ten people in my group. But you must know that there were other people living in that village, people who were permanently residents in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, moving on to the 24th of May, 1992, do you recall the attack or the shelling of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I was just there in the village of Javori. Around 1.00 past midnight, we heard shots. It was barage fire from automatic weapons from Donja Garevci. From the village of Orlovci, fire was opened on Kozarac which lasted for about five or ten minutes, and then everything Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was silent again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How many people were with you at that --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Five or six of us in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How long did the shelling or the shooting go on?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: At that moment, it went on for about five or ten minutes, and then there was a lull, and then it was continued in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How long did that take, go on for?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Later, the shelling of Kozarac, the continued shelling of Kozarac lasted for about 48 hours. There was constant shelling, and shells were coming from a number of different sides. So I'd say about 48 hours altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: That means it went on until the 26th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see any casualties?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Where I was in that village, a shell fell, and six fellows were killed by that shell. They were sitting together near the village, and a shell landed just in the middle of that group, and those people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know as to what was taking place in the other parts of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I know that fire was coming from all the different directions. I was informed that infantry and artillery had set out from Omarska and that the civilians who tried to protect the Jakupovici and Kamicani villages, those lines had been penetrated and the population was retreating towards the centre of Kozarac. The same thing was happening in Kozarusa, too. So the whole population of Kozarac and the surrounding villages was retreating towards the centre of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What did you do in the place you were in, from Javori?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: As we had already seen that Kozarac would be taken, that it would fall, a friend of mine who was a reserve police officer and myself, we went to a motel near a village where the Kozarac hospital had been moved to. There were lots of wounded people there. I tried to find Becir Medunjanin and Sead Cirkin and see what was to be done, but then I was told that the personnel there had no idea where Becir was. The Prijedor authorities had told the Kozarac police to hand in their weapons so that the wounded civilians would be admitted to the hospital in Prijedor. Later, I returned to the village of Javori and informed the people there roughly about what was happening. Then they left the village, and we also retreated towards the centre of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, on the 26th of May, 1992, late that day, did a large number of the population in Kozarac surrender?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, most of the population in Kozarac surrendered. They left the centre. But a smaller area, the place where I lived in that area, there were between five and ten thousand civilians in that area, women, children, in the cellars of the houses there. The army had already entered the centre of Kozarac, the place called Stari Grad in Kozarac. And together with my relative, Hamdija Mrkovic [as interpreted], I discussed the possibilities of what could be done. But he said that if the shelling continued, probably the consequences would be that a large number of civilians, women and children -- that a large number of civilians would end up as victims, would be killed. And as he worked with the police, for the police, he felt responsible and thought he was supposed to do something. From where we were staying at that point, he saw a Serb tank manned by Zoran Karlica, a man he used to know very well. He decided to a make white flag. He sat on a motorbike and went towards the tank. From what I could see, he was talking to Zoran Karlica on the tank. When he returned, he told me that he had received orders to take his car, his wife and children, that he had to form a convoy and lead the convoy, that he was supposed to lead the convoy and no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Arifagic, did you know where this convoy headed towards, went towards, and what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: It was explained to him that all those who wished to surrender could join the convoy and that there would be a cease-fire during that period. So these people followed him and surrendered. I learned that they reached the main road, the Banja Luka/Prijedor main road, that the women and children were separated from the men, and that the women and children were then sent to the Trnopolje camp while the men were sent to Keraterm and Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May this be a convenient time to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. I have asked to start this part of the hearing in the absence of the witness. I don't really know how come that none of the parties requested this, that this witness could be introduced under 92 bis. We can read on the summaries the words "92 bis" but evidently we rechecked during the break, there was no application for 92 bis. Could we please know why, and is there a possibility, and I would ask for this, that we really concentrate on issues not yet covered exhaustively by former witnesses. It does, of course, not mean that we are convinced by all that what has been said in the past by other witnesses, but we have to avoid too much -- too many repetitions. So therefore, we should really concentrate on the absolutely necessary in the future, if this is feasible for you. But please, if you could indicate the reasons why we didn't get an application for this witness under 92 bis, what are the core issues that we are aware of these core issues we have to expect today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour, as I am dealing with this witness. I too, saw that he was going to become a witness under 92 bis, but we did not make that application. He would, as you would see under the 65 ter, would testify with regard to some of the matters that I have already led, and he would be testifying with regard to his experience in the Keraterm camp where it is alleged in the indictment under paragraphs 46 and 47 certain massacres at that took place in Keraterm. There had not been any other witnesses who have testified to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. One can read this already from the summary, but I think it's not necessary to touch upon once again the taking over the Kozarac television broadcast tower, whether this happened or not, and all the issues related to the area of Kozarac as such. And therefore, I invite, if possible -- of course, I can't restrict you if you believe there's something new in addition to the area as regards the area of Kozarac. But please, then concentrate on the situation in the Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I would, Your Honour. I have tried my best to restrict the areas. Unwillingly sometimes the witness would speak about certain -- and to have a sequence, I have been asking these questions. But I will make it -- I will try my best to keep or restrict my examination and only refer to the main matters that would be necessary for the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The usher may bring in, please, the witness again. The OTP may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I start, Your Honour, I have been informed by the interpreters to caution the witness to slow down a little bit while he answers. Could I do that, or Your Honour may.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, could you, when you answer the questions, please speak slowly and slow down possibly that the interpreters could keep up with you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, we were -- very quickly, we'll go through some areas before we come to the arrest. You were among some of the people in Kozarac who did not surrender or who did not want to surrender. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Why didn't you surrender?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I wanted to wait and see what would happen because I knew that if I surrendered, that would be it. It was this feeling of uncertainty that I had that made me try and stick around for a while. I still believed that we would be given the opportunity of staying at our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did the group that you were in -- you were in a group of people from Kozarac, the villagers, that retreated to Mount Kozara. While you were towards Mount Kozara, you were ambushed at a place called Zeciji Kamen. Do you recall that event?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We were ambushed, and in this column of people there were women, children, and civilians. We tried to cross the road leading to Mrakovica from Kozarac, and at the location that we call Zeciji Kamen, we were shot at. According to what I know, 120 people were captured in this incident. They were subsequently taken to Benkovac. Some of them were immediately executed, and some were later transferred to the Omarska camp. Others, women and children, continued towards Kozara Mount. We made contact with Kapetan Cirkin. We found Becir Medunjanin and others. We contacted them because we wanted them to tell us what should we do next and what the next plan would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Arifagic, if we go ahead, proceed further, is it correct that you were arrested on the 14th of June, 1992, at Mujkanovici?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And until the 14th of June, 1992, until your arrest, you were in the forest?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you armed, or did you -- what did you do with your -- did you have a weapon with you?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: We had hunting weapons which we kept for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you get rid of the weapon?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I discarded my weapon because I decided to cross the Prijedor/Banja Luka Road at one point and went to the village of Mujkanovici. The reason I did that was because I had already received information that my wife, my daughter, my mother, my father, and my brother were already in the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now during this time, did you see any Serb soldiers in the village of Kozarac or the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I was able to see Serb soldiers to loot systematically the Kozarac town and the surrounding villages on a daily basis. Anything that was of any value was taken away, driven away on tractors and other vehicles, household appliances were looted. Some of the machines were left in place, the things they couldn't take with them. Those were subsequently destroyed. So the town of Kozarac and the surrounding villages were systematically looted and set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, going to the date of the 14th of June, 1992, could you very briefly explain as to what happened at Mujkanovici?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I went to the village of Mujkanovici because my mother's sister lived there. The village is situated in the vicinity of the Trnopolje camp, and I wanted to meet with my mother there. However, on that day, in the village of Mujkanovici and the surrounding villages, the so-called cleansing occurred. That's how the Serbs called them. These villages were encircled and men were systematically taken away from their homes. The women and children were given opportunity to remain and continue living there in their homes alone without men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when you were arrested, were you arrested by Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How many people were there with you ultimately when you were taken away from the village?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Approximately 40 people in a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, proceeding further, without going into details with regard to what happened during that time, is it correct that from there onwards this group of people that was taken away from the village of Mujkanovici ordered to march towards Kamicani?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: On your way, you all were beaten, you all were asked to sing songs, Serbian songs, by the Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And ultimately, you were loaded or you were asked -- ordered to board a bus. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It happened in the village of Kamicani at a checkpoint where we were stopped. On that occasion, we were harassed and beaten. And me and a young man who was standing at the head of the column were taken away. From what we could hear from the soldiers who were taking us, we thought we would be executed. They said that now you will see how people are executed. But we were taken to a house, a nearby house, where we were ordered to load some household appliances -- unload some household appliances from a truck. Later we heard that a bus had arrived, and apparently the two of us were to be taken back. They made us run. They told us that those, the one who is the last would be beaten up. I was the last one, and I got beaten up, but I managed to get on to the bus which continued on its way to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, the bus that you talk about, did you recognise these buses, or did you know as to where they came from?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: The bus belonged to the Autotransport company from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see any sign written on the bus?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a sign on the bus, on the sides of the bus "Autotransport Company." I'm familiar with this bus because I used to take it when I went to secondary school to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, to proceed further skipping some area, you were taken in the buses to -- first to Omarska camp. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And from there, you all proceeded again, the bus went towards a place called the Keraterm ceramic factory. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, going into details at the camp, could you describe what you refer to as the Keraterm ceramic factory, its location.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: It is located at the outskirts of Prijedor going from the direction of Kozarac, near Cirkin Polje on the right side of the main Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. road. Keraterm is a ceramic tiles factory. It produced and distributed ceramic tiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, talking about the location, is it correct if I say that this was a location on the Prijedor/Banja Luka main road?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could anyone passing on this main road, the Prijedor/Banja Luka Road, see any persons who were in the vicinity of the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When you were detained in the camp, did you see movement on the Prijedor/Banja Luka Road, people going in vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, we would see them very often, in particular on those occasions when we were taken out to get some food, of which we received always very little. But it was at that time that we were able to see the road. In those days, there was very often fighting in the area of Derventa, and every time a column of vehicles would pass along the road coming from the direction of Banja Luka going towards Prijedor, we were able to see them. We were there. We could see them pass by. We could hear the soldiers singing songs and motioning with this traditional Serb salute.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you, in your estimate, say as to how far this Keraterm camp was from Prijedor the town?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Taking into account the location of the town hall, the centre of the Prijedor town, the police station, not more than 2, 2 and a half kilometres, in my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, when you were brought to the camp on the 14th of June, 1992, when the buses stopped, were you ordered to get out of the bus?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And what did they ask you to do?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Two Serb soldiers entered the bus, one on the front entrance and the other at the back entrance, and they told us to leave the bus in groups of five or six people. We were made to raise our hands, and we were searched at that moment. Then we were ordered to lie down on the concrete surface and to place our hands at the backs of our heads. The people who were escorting us -- well, we couldn't see them because we were lying down. But we surely did feel their blows and kicks. What I remember very well is soldiers jumping on our backs, going from one to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: After that, were you ordered to go to any other location or any room in the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: My group was ordered to get up and to run to Room Number 2. They indicated to us where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour, at this stage request your permission to use an exhibit which has been already marked and admitted, Exhibit Number S15-1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And also S15-33 to be given to the witness. If that could be put on the ELMO, S15-1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recognise this -- what is depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Is this the place that you referred to as Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you kindly point out to the place that you referred to as -- if I may ask you to use S15-33. That would be very much appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The witness is shown S15-33.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you point out to the place that you referred to as Room 2.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you, in the time that you spent at the camp, get to know there were other rooms that were also called by numbers? If I may use, call it Room 1, did you know that there was a place which was called Room 1 in the camp, and could you kindly point it out?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You can use a pen or just your finger if it's difficult with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness points out to the extreme glass area as Room 1, and then the adjoining portion as Room 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Then, Witness, did you get to know that there was a place also called as Room 3?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Before you came to Room 3, there was an entrance to the toilet. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So noting that place, the entrance to the toilet, could you kindly point out to the place, the door, of Room 3, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness indicated --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: It looks as if it's a metal door. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you were asked to go to Room 2. And when you went into the room which is called Room 2, did you see any other persons who were there at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, people had been put up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When you say "people," did you get to know who these people were and what they were doing there?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: People were there who had been brought there in the same way they were detained in the camp, mostly people from the surrounding villages of Prijedor. A small number of people from Kozarac, and then from Puharska, Gornji and Donji, from Prijedor town centre, from villages like Rizvanovici, Hambarine, Gomjenica, mostly. Villages near Prijedor Municipality mostly populated by Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, now you said that you were asked to go to Room 2. Did the others who came with you, the group of almost 40 people, were also sent to the same room?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What would your approximate estimate be of the people all together in the Room 2 at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: At that time, perhaps 200, 250, 300 people. I didn't exactly keep count, but the room was full.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And how big was this Room 2, very briefly, if you could explain.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: It was an irregular square, perhaps 30 by 20 metres on the inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When you were inside the Room 2, could you see outside? Could you see what was happening outside while you were in Room 2?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everything happening at the gate, at the checkpoint, on the way in, the same things were happening outside Room 1, Room 2, and the other rooms. You could see a part of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, very quickly, could you explain as to what happened in the night. Were you called out that night with a group of people that came with you and what were you ordered to do?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Sometime in the evening, that means earlier, it was night, and then all the people who came in the last bus, that was us. We were called outside. And once outside, we were ordered outside Rooms 1 and 2 to lie down on the floor, on the asphalt floor, and put our hands behind our head. Then there were beatings and maltreatments, and I was asked to admit, to confess that I was a Green Beret. They beat me. My head, my arms, and my knew were injured. They beat me in order to confess that I was a Green Beret. I tried to put up with the pain, but at some point, I'm not sure why, I told them if I have a green beret I wouldn't be in the camp right now. I would be out in the woods. And then the man who was beating me ordered me to go to the bedroom. And then at the door I was stopped again and I was asked to explain, that is, they asked me about a man who owned a cafe in Kozarac by his name. I couldn't remember the cafe, but after they explained everything to me, I remembered and I told them I knew the man but that I didn't know where he was. And at the same time, just outside Room Number 2, one of the people who arrived there with me Adnan Kljucanin was being beaten. He was lying on the floor. I was standing perhaps a metre away from him. They were hitting him on the kidneys mostly, and they wanted him, too, to confess, that he was a Green Beret. Later, they asked me whether I knew him. I said I did and that as far as I knew, he was not a member of any army or anything. And then at that point, I was ordered to go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Arifagic, did you sustain or suffer any permanent injuries by this beating?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, my head was injured. I was bleeding profusely. My left arm was swollen three or four fingers. It was just a mass of blood. I didn't know what had happened really. I had an injury on my knee also. That wound, too, was bleeding. And during the night, it was hot. The pain was unbearable. And then when the injuries got cold the next day, the pain, again, was great. But then the camp inmates advised me that I should apply some cold water on to my wounds. They told me that would ease my pain. I tried that, but it didn't help very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Next morning, you were taken to hospital with some other detainees. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You were taken in a van driven by a person whom you knew before. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were taken away in some sort of a van or a minibus. The man who was driving, I didn't know his name but I know that he had worked as a conductor for Autotransport. On the passenger seat there was Zoran Zigic holding an automatic rifle, and we were seated in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you make out or know any other detainees who were in the bus with you who went to the hospital that day?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Emsud Bahonjic who had arrived in the camp earlier, and he had many injuries. He was in a critical state. I think there was Jasmin Colic there and other people whose names I can't remember also. But these were people who were all severely injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You said that there was a person by the name of Emsud Bahonjic and he had many injuries. Do you know as to how he was injured?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Later, when we were returned from the hospital to the camp, I talked to Emsud. We knew each other quite well from before. And he told me that at the entrance gate to the camp when passing the cabin that was on the way in, Zigic came up to him, tapped him on the shoulder, told him that he was his sniper, that he knew he had had a sniper and that he was a sniper. And then he said that Zoran Zigic and Dusan Knezevic, Dusa, systematically took him out for beatings and in the end forced him to sign a statement in which he confessed to having been a sniper, a sharp shooter. And then they told him afterwards that he would not be maltreated any more. But they only used these signed statements to continue torturing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know whether Emsud survived the camp or what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Emsud did not survive. After a couple of days, one afternoon, Emsud died. And we carried his body out towards the guards' cabin. We laid him down there and at night, when we went outside the bedrooms to get some water and to go to the toilet, we saw that his body had been laid in a place we used to refer to as the garbage dump. There was only a roof there on concrete pillars. That was a place to deposit construction material and other sorts of waste. We saw that his body had been abandoned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, at the hospital, were you treated? Were you given any medicine?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No. All I got was I met a nurse who knew my sister-in-law and some other relatives of mine. She asked questions about her. This is Hamdija Arifagic's wife I'm talking about. She tried to obtain information about them, but could not. And then she told me that she would try to help me. What she could do is she gave me some sort of a gauze, a bandage. I put it over my head, and then she gave me another bandage for my arm. She told me to rinse it in cold water and that she would help me to dress the wound, but there was not much more she could do. And she did the same with my leg. And then after that, I returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Arifagic, while your stayed in the camp, in Keraterm, did you observe beatings?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, people were beaten, especially at night. Names were called out, and they were called to come out of their buildings, and then you could hear cries and moans, people weeping. Some of those people never returned, but those who did return were usually in a very bad shape with their arms or legs broken, with bruises.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see dead bodies in the camp and they being removed?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where did you see these dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Most of these bodies I saw after the massacre the first night in Room Number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, I would come to that in a little while. Other than the Room 3 incident that we would speak about, did you see any other bodies in the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were people who after being taken out at night and killed, their bodies were usually dumped in the place we used to refer to as the garbage dump. One night, Fikret Avdic was beaten. The man who was in charge of the bedroom and who was in charge of contact with the guards, he brought him in. But after 20 minutes, Fikret died. In the morning, his body was taken out of the room and dumped in that same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, very quickly, could you say as to who were the people who were responsible for these beatings? Did you know any of them by names?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: For us, those people were guard shift leaders and the guards there. We didn't see anything else nor could we obtain any further information. It all depended on who was standing guard, who was on the shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recall -- before we leave this area, do you recall two policemen who were former policemen being brought to the camp in uniform as detainees? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know the names of these two people, persons?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: One of them was Drago, and the other I think was Fikret.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know them before the war?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew them by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: The person whom you refer to as Fikret, is it correct if I say he was Esad?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: That's possible. I think his name was Fikret, but I'd only seen him several times.
