utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you explain very quickly and briefly what happened to them when they were brought to the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: They were brought there wearing police uniforms, the uniforms that the Serbian police was using at that time. They had military boots on their feet. And what they told us is that they had signed the oath of loyalty required right away, on the first day, to the authorities in Prijedor, the people who were in power then. And that after that day, they had been working. But on that day, they told us they were disarmed and brought to the Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And what happened to them thereafter?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: That night, their names were called out. They were taken out of the room. They were the only two people called out. They were outside, and we could hear clearly that they were being beaten. You could hear their cries. Fikret or whatever you think his name was came back alive, but Drago didn't. What happened to him, I can only assume that perhaps he was killed. But Fikret told us the next morning that Drago had, in fact, been killed, that they beat them both with chains and with metal rods. They made them walk on all fours around the building. Drago succumbed to the beatings, and Fikret, I'm not sure how he made it but...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Arifagic, did you see your father being brought to the camp on the 1st or 2nd of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see him being beaten?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... And who beat him?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: He was 62 at that time. In my statement, I said that he was in the Trnopolje camp. As he was 62 years old, he managed to obtain from the Serbian Red Cross and the people who ran the camp a certificate allowing him to take my mother, his wife, and to look for accommodation in Durajci at my grandfather's house. It's one of the villages nearby. That's the village my mother came from. On the 21st of July, that was the last village to be cleansed, the Serbian army came and he was arrested alongside with the other male villagers. He was taken towards the Trnopolje camp. He was beaten and tortured there, and then from Trnopolje, they were transferred in buses to the Keraterm camp. He told me that at the entrance gate to the Keraterm camp, two Serb soldiers boarded the bus and asked him to come out. One of them made him leave the bus and the other was trying to get him back on the bus. And all the while they were systematically beating him. One of them accusing him of having killed his grandfather Radovan on Mount Kozara in 1942. However in 1942, my father was only 12 years old, so it's difficult to see how this could have happened. I found him in Room 3. His nose had been broken. I told him to come to Room Number 2 where I was staying but he was scared. He said they would kill me if I go. And then I told him: "You'll be killed anyway. The only chance you still have is to come to the room where I am staying." As he was a sick man and he was having stomach trouble, I thought that if he comes to my room, I can try to see to his wounds, to dress his wounds, and that maybe he would stand the chance of living a day longer perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Later on, he was transferred to Trnopolje again. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was taken away around the 15th of June, the 15th of July from Keraterm. We didn't know where he was being taken to. But I later found out that he was brought to Trnopolje. One thing perhaps I should point out, if I may, the certificate he got from the Serb authorities he showed the soldiers that he had been released. But they told him that he could stick it up somewhere, so due to his being naive, he ended up back inside the camp for a second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, I will take your attention to the 20th or 21st of July, 1992. Do you recall the prisoners who were there already in Room Number 3 being asked to go to other rooms or Room 3 being cleared during that time?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had orders to make room, that some of the people from Room Number 3 were to be transferred to our room, and we did so. It was difficult to see where exactly they would put these people, but they were just simply crammed into the room, into the Rooms 2 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: After this, did you observe people being brought in buses to the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you explain what you noticed or observed.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: People were being brought in buses past the checkpoint on the way in. Something was being written down there, and their documents were being checked. Anyway, these people were put in Room Number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you get to know from where these people came from?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, the night when the room was filled, when we couldn't go out -- when we went out of the room, I met some people I knew. And those were mostly people from the area we referred to as Brdo. It's a group of four or five villages across the Sana River just above Prijedor. We called the area Brdo because it's on some sort of an elevation above Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see the people who were brought there being searched? You said that you saw them being checked and their documents being looked into. Did you get to know as to what they did with these documents?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know what was done, but I knew that their documents were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: From the prisoners or the detainees who were brought in buses?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Those who came on the buses, and some of the prisoners, too, who were later brought in lorries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, these people who were brought in that day were sent to Room 3. Were they allowed to come out and contact the other people in the camp that day?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, on that day, they were. I met some people I knew. I talked to these people. I know that those were people from that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were they allowed to come out of the Room 3 thereafter?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No. Later they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you allowed to go out, the people in Room 2 and Room 1 and Room 4?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: A day or two later after they had been brought in, we did go out occasionally, but those from Room Number 3 didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And on a particular -- couple of days after these people were brought in from the Brdo area, were you all ordered to go to the room early and were locked in thereafter?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, just before nightfall, we were told to go into the bedroom, to stay calm, to face the wall. There was a grid that was closed all the time on Bedroom Number 2. Only some air could get into the room, but on the other side there was a metal door that could be shut.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you hear any movement, particularly late in the evening that day?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. During that night, around 9.00 or 10.00, you could hear the sound of vehicles coming, lorries. There was a lot of commotion. We could hear the army enter the camp, and then you could hear voices yelling. People were trying to agree on something apparently, but we just stayed calm in the bedroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you hear shooting after some time? Could you explain what you heard?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: What I heard and the rest of us around 11.00 perhaps, or later, I couldn't tell you what time it was exactly. But suddenly, there was a burst of gunfire, not only from light weapons, automatic rifles. So probably those were heavy weapons being used. We could hear sounds of metal breaking, glass shattered. You could hear bullets flying in through the roof. And at one point we heard a voice saying, Don't touch bedroom number 1 and 2. But then we heard cries and moans. It was a turmoil. We heard terrible cries. We could hear sounds of things breaking, being shattered. People were calling each other and asking for help. But we, on the other side, we just kept calm all the time. We were afraid even to breathe too loud.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How long did the shooting last?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: The shooting lasted for about half an hour, an hour, perhaps that long.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What did you observe the next morning?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: The next morning, when the doors to our room opened, we saw guards who were looking for volunteers. They said explicitly that they were looking for volunteers that were not afraid of the dead. I think that two men went from my room; they were asked to go to Room Number 3. We could see from our room, because the doors were open at the time, that a large number of bodies were outside Room Number 3, that the whole area was covered in blood. The people who worked inside, we could see them. A very long trailer truck arrived, a 20 or 30-metre long trailer truck, and the bodies were loaded on to this truck. So we were able to observe all this, and we thought that perhaps our turn would come the next day. When this work was over, and when the truck left as it was moving out from the compound of the camp -- I mean, we could see directly the checkpoint from our room, something that keeps haunting me to this day. Something that I often try hard to forget, but I've realised that this is something that I will have to live with. It was the sight of a truck moving away and leaving traces of blood behind. There was blood dripping from the truck, and we could see that it was heavily loaded. After the truck left, a fire engine arrived; that is, a vehicle which had all kinds of cleaning and washing devices attached to it. They tried to wash the area with this vehicle. They tried to remove the blood and to wash off the blood of this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, were you able to talk to someone, a detainee, who helped in the removal of the dead, the dead bodies, and did he say approximately as to how many bodies were loaded that day?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I talked to a man whom I knew very well. His name was Jasim Causevic. He was the brother of my brother-in-law, so we knew each other very well. He was one of the volunteers who volunteered to load the dead because those people used to be his neighbours. He told me that there were four rows of bodies piled on top of one another. Whether we are talking about hundreds of bodies, I don't know. I don't know whether those were just parts of bodies or the whole bodies. I'm not sure, but this is what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, after the area was cleaned, the same night, the night the area was cleaned, did you hear again another shooting that took place?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The next night at approximately the same time, the same thing happened again. But unlike the previous night, it didn't last that long. However, at one point, we heard a voice shouting out: "What are we going to do? There are survivors here." And then we heard individual shots, and I started counting the shots. I thought that those were the shots to finish off the survivors. I tried to count them. There were perhaps 42 or 43 shots that I could count, but I'm not sure. After that, everything became quiet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see the dead being taken away?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The same thing happened the next morning, except that the next morning a smaller truck arrived; it was a Zastava 640. The bodies were, again, loaded on to this truck. And then after that, they wanted the people from Rooms 1, 2, and 4 who had wounds to come out. Many of us were wounded. We had various kinds of injuries, cuts, and bruises. So these people came out, and they were also -- they also boarded this truck. And when this was over, even the people, the six people who had collected the bodies, were loaded on to this truck. I saw Jasim Causevic leaving on this truck. He was the last one on the right side. He was sitting on the truck, and he still had this uniform, his official uniform that he had as an employee of this factory where he worked in Prijedor. And they were all taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, when you were allowed to go after the first shooting, the Room 3 massacre that took place on the first night -- when you went out, did you see in the area, other than the machine-gun which was permanently there, an additional machine-gun which was brought to the camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Outside Room 3, there was a path, a road, leading away from the factory. And at the distance of some 20 or 30 metres, there was a table, an ordinary table. And there was a chair behind it. There was a huge floodlight on the right-hand side which can provide very strong light. And the heavy machine-gun was there. It was an 84 millimetre machine-gun which was facing Room Number 3, pointing at Room Number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just interrupt for a better understanding. Witness, you told us after this incident, this first incident and all the bodies were removed by this huge lorry, the same happened the next day. Does this mean that Room Number 3 was refilled, or the victims were such from other rooms of this camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The people in question were the survivors of the massacre that occurred on the first night in Room 3. So the same happened again on the next day, but I'm talking about the group of people who had survived the first night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So we have first the group you could only give us an estimate of the number. Then there were survivors. And then you heard, just to be -- just for clarification, then you heard a voice saying: "There are still survivors." And then you heard individual shooting. So there was another group of individual survivors, all from Room Number 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me try to explain. After the first night, the killing or the shooting at Room 3 occurred again the next Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. night. The one who said those words, that there were still survivors left, was probably referring to the people who had been wounded, the people who were lying there but were not dead. So the next night, other people were killed, and these other people were again loaded on to the smaller truck, together with the people who had collected the bodies and the people who were detained in other rooms and were wounded, and were taken away together with them. After the second night, there was a small group of people still in Room 3 who had survived both nights. So Room Number 3 was full at the beginning. During the first night, a number of people were killed. Then the second night, additional number of people were killed. And then a smaller group of people remained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, the person whom you referred to as Jasim Causevic, did you see thereafter, after you saw him last leaving in that truck after the second night?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. His name is Jasim Causevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you spoke about the shootings that took place in Room 3. Did you know a person by the name of Simo Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know him before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know what position he held after the takeover in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: He was a commander with the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see him in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "He was the commander of the SUP."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see him in the Keraterm camp after the shooting?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where did you see him, and when was it?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I think it was either the next day or two or three days later. At any rate, he was at the Keraterm camp. He was standing outside Room Number 1, to the right side of Room Number 1, with a group of people. I remember we were given an opportunity to get out at that moment, and those who were closer to the guards were able to approach him. And apparently, we received promises -- we received assurances from Drljaca. He said something to the effect that this should not have happened, that better control would be soon in place, and that we had his assurances that we would not be harmed again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who were the others who were with him? Did you recognise any of those people?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Most of them were guards at the camp, but there were other individuals with him. I remember a man who did not have -- who had only one hand. I don't remember whether it was the left one or the right one, but I remember that he was there. And another one who was a physician.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When you say a physician, you mean to say is he a doctor from the Prijedor hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: It's possible that he worked in Prijedor. I think he was a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When did you leave Keraterm, the camp Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: We left Keraterm around the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: We were taken to the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you taken in buses with others who were in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Me and a number of other detainees were taken to the Trnopolje camp. However, before that, some hundred or hundred and thirty people were told to get their belongings and to come out. These people were loaded on to two or three buses. They were escorted by the guards who immediately started beating them. They said that the buses would pass by the sleeping rooms and that people should board the bus as it approaches their room. And that is how a convoy was formed at the exit of the Keraterm camp. We were transported to Trnopolje via Cirkin Polje and Gornji and Donji Garevci. And we eventually reached the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Arafagic, in your opinion, who was in charge of the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Kuruzovic. It's not only my opinion. Everybody knew that he was the one who was calling the shots there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know him before?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I may have by sight, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How long were you kept in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Until the 1st of October the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When you had to leave the camp on the 1st of October, were you asked to do anything to leave the camp? Were you asked to sign any documents?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Well, if we wanted to be registered with the International Red Cross and leave the camp, we were asked to fill in some forms. We had to submit a request for departure to the appropriate authorities in Prijedor, which is what we all did. I think I still have this decision written in Cyrillic script whereby pursuant to my request for leaving the territory of -- the territory of Prijedor Municipality, this departure was authorised, and also that I thereby relinquished all my property to the authorities in Prijedor. Anyway, this is what we all signed, and it was only after that that we were allowed to leave the camp by bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: That concludes the examination-in-chief. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you for our better understanding to introduce the sketch drawn by the witness, the 23rd of October, 1994. And that with the assistance of this sketch where we only can find the B/C/S declaration of the rooms and other facilities, what is the meaning and the situation of the rooms in this area. Could this please be presented on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour, is it with the number 02015259, that's the English version; and in B/C/S, 0174439? Is it a sketch with regard to the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. If this is shown to the witness, may I ask a couple of questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't know whether others in this room are in a better position than me, but I have first of all the B/C/S, and then, yes, some English translation, put it this way, ending with number 259. If you just could go briefly through this sketch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May I? Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recognise this sketch? Was it drawn by you?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the sketch which was the number 00174439. Now, could you kindly show which room you refer to as Room Number 1, point out what you refer to as Room Number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Room Number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you see Room 3 and the place that you have marked as WC?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you see --

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Is there any correction that you need to do?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: These two locations have been confused. The toilet is actually behind, but they are next to each other. This is probably a mistake in drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What you -- if I get you correctly, the toilet must be before Room Number 3? You get the toilet, and then after that the Room Number 3. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. You have to swap these two locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And then next to the Room Number 3, you have the place that you refer to as Room Number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: If I may ask you, there were machine-gun nests, what you referred to as machine-gun nests. Could you point out to those places? I'm not talking about the additional machine-gun which you referred to in your testimony, but the permanently -- where two machine-guns were placed. Could you kindly point out to those places, please.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: One was here. Outside Room Number 3 looking from the right-hand side. There was a small hut here for the guards to protect them from rain, I think. And the other one was here at this corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: If I correct the first portion of your answer, the first machine-gun area that you showed was not in front of Room Number 3; it was in front of Room Number 1, which is towards the Banja Luka/Prijedor Road. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was always there. And then the second one which was also permanent is this one, where the machine-gun nest was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: That was in front of Room Number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: This permanent location was in front of the toilet, outside the toilet on the left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And you spoke about an additional machine-gun which has been placed on a table and a search light. Is it also marked on the map?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Which is where it says "machine-gun and a spotlight used for massacre in Room 3." Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Does that satisfy Your Honour? Thank you. That concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You tender this as evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I may. I did not want to because as there was an error with regard to Room 3 and the toilet. Now it has been -- as it has been rectified, may I have the next number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be S277. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence as S277A and B correspondingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.58 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Before I give the floor to the Defence, may the usher please, once again, present Document Exhibit Number S277 on the ELMO, just for clarification, because I am afraid there was a misunderstanding on the transcript. To the best of your recollection, could you please tell us as regards the situation of the restroom, toilet, was it situated between Room 2 and 3, or 2 and 4? Was there access to this toilet from two rooms, and please, point once again with your pointer to the exact point where you recall that there was the access to this toilet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The toilet, it's true that it was after Room 2, but this part of the Keraterm factory here protrudes a little bit. So you can't say that it was immediately after -- immediately next to Room Number 2, but here, at this corner. And then after the toilet come the rooms Number 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it was not in front -- as seen now from our perspective, in front of Room 3, but between Room 2 and 3. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification to the transcript. Now, the floor is open for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Arifagic.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We speak the same language. They refer to it here as B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's probably true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There might be some difficulty when I pose the question. Please, make a short pause following my question so that the interpreters may have enough time to interpret. Also, if you see me waiting for some time after you've completed your answer, that doesn't mean I'm not happy with your answer; that only means I'm waiting for the interpreters to finish their work. Can we begin now?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You returned to Kozarac in December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you work in Croatia before that time?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the National Guard while you were in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you bring back from Croatia the weapon that you had used there?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No, perhaps I owe you an explanation. The seat of my company was actually in Croatia, but as I have previously said in my statement, I spent five and a half years on a construction site in Libya with my company.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter would like to correct the date in the first answer. It's 1991, not 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please explain where you obtained the weapons from, the weapons you had in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: The hunting rifle I got from one of the villagers. Plenty of people in Kozarac used to hunt, so many people had hunting rifles. It was a hunting rifle. So when someone came to relieve me at the guard duty Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. where I was, I just leave him the rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Following the 30th of April, 1992, how many members of the police force were in Kozarac? I'm talking about both the active and the reserve-duty police officers.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I could not give you the exact number, but there was a high number of police officers in Kozarac at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with some witnesses that there were about 100 police officers?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: That sounds possible. I did not deal with the police, so I can't tell you exactly how many people there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that part of the police equipment -- that the automatic rifle also belongs to the police equipment?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I know that the police had weapons, but I thought that was only for wartime. I did not think that they carried these weapons in peacetime also.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the existence of the Territorial Defence of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: If you mean -- yes, if you mean the Territorial Defence that existed in Kozarac for a while. However, it had been there in Kozarac for a long time, long before the takeover and the beginning of the conflict. The Territorial Defence was led by people who were members of the reserve forces of the JNA wearing uniforms of the reserve forces. So the weapons they had were weapons that belonged to the Territorial Defence. But as far as I know all those weapons were later turned in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "the weapons were turned in later," which moment exactly are you talking about? Which point in time?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I know that the Territorial Defence existed in Kozarac for at least half a year before the conflict in Kozarac broke out. Who activated the TO forces, I don't know, because at that point no one was even thinking about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that the Kozarac area was surrounded by ten Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: About ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said you had set up checkpoints facing Serb villages in order to protect yourselves?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: You can choose to call it a checkpoint if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Or guard points.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were in the Kozarac area, and we were simply observing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that there were at least ten such points?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: You mean around the whole of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: People mainly patrolled of their own initiative through the Kozarac area trying to prevent anything bad from happening and watching who was entering the villages -- the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that the Serb media, particularly after the repeater on Mount Kozara had been taken, referred to the Bosnian army as the "Green Berets"?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that this was -- that this was happening as early as February or March 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: That sounds possible because even that early in Bijeljina and some other places, conflicts had broken out. That was a name they used referring to an army. They called this army the Green Berets, whether this was such thing as a BH army or not, probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, did you know or did you learn later about the existence of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I knew about the TO, but I didn't know about the existence of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you learn later on about the existence of the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, after I had left the camp, I heard stories about the Green Berets. But while I was still staying there, I knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Bosniaks and Croats refused to respond to the mobilisation call-ups in 1991. Did you know whether anyone was arrested because of that? Do you know of any such specific cases?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Not where I lived, but people used to hide, and they simply didn't want to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 19 of today's transcript, you speak about a helicopter that landed in Balte. And you say that this helicopter brought weapons to the inhabitants of Balte. You say a relative of yours who worked as a police officer in Kozarac informed you about this. When did you learn this from your relative? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: That was immediately prior to the takeover of Prijedor, before the conflict broke out and before the Serb authorities took power in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement of 1994 to officials of this Tribunal, did you not state that you had no idea what was in that helicopter?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: That's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you something concerning the oath of loyalty. Were all inhabitants of Kozarac required to sign the oath of loyalty to Serb authorities, or were only police officers required to do so? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: As far as I knew, probably what was required was the whole of -- for the whole of Kozarac to sign an oath of loyalty. What was implicit in that request, I couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You never actually saw this piece of paper that was to be signed, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you learn about this request?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Becir Medunjanin and the people who held appointments, elected appointments, in Kozarac were in permanent contact with the authorities in Prijedor. And after that, they informed the people of Kozarac. They asked for an opinion whether maybe in the name of the people of Kozarac an oath of loyalty was to be signed; the people, however, refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you did not hear about this over the radio; Becir Medunjanin told you.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Later I heard over the radio, too, that the population of the surrounding villages - but that was some time before - was called upon to sign an oath of loyalty to the authorities in Prijedor. But during the war and during the events preceding the war, I was informed by Becir Medunjanin that we were actually required to sign this oath of loyalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In connection with this, you say: "We had information that some villages had, in fact, signed this oath of loyalty and turned in their weapons, but that despite having signed the oath of loyalty, they were later attacked." Can you tell us which villages exactly you had in mind when you said this?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Hambarine, for example. We heard that they had turned in their weapons and signed the oath of loyalty, but several days later, we could see the villages burning from Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see Hambarine burning only two or three days before Kozarac was attacked?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the incident that took place at the checkpoint in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: They did say something about that on the radio, about the checkpoint being attacked, but I did not know anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony, and even now, you mentioned that you were given information about some things by Becir Medunjanin, special information concerning negotiations with SDS officials. You claim that after every round of negotiations, they would go and visit the people on the ground explaining the situation, the situation at any given moment in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us how this information was passed on? Were meetings organised, or did they just go from house to house?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No, we mostly did this in the halls of culture we had in our villages. People would assemble, then they would explain the situation, they wanted the people's opinion, and then they would just leave and go somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how many such meetings do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: In the part of town where I lived, we had two or three such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us who attended these meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: The meetings I'm talking about were attended by Becir Medunjanin and Besim Alic. The meetings were also attended by the local population of the respective villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "the local population," do you mean military-aged men, or do you also imply that women and children attended?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I think there was no need for children to attend such meetings, so mostly these meetings were attended by men.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say you stood guard in the part of the Kozarac area in the village of Javori.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you live in Javori?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No, I don't, but I live in the village that's next to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was it who decided or ordered you to be in Javori? Who assigned you to Javori?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No one in particular. We agreed amongst ourselves that there was no need for guards to sit in front of their individual houses, that we should go to the outskirts of Kozarac and stand guard there and try to protect the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anyone organise shifts of guards?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: It was usually done on our own initiative. When we finished our shift, another group would come, and they would take over our weapons so that the guard duty could continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sead Cirkin, did he make any decisions in relation to these guards?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Well, in view of his position, that is, the position that he used to have in the JNA, yes, because we all believed that he would be able to do something to avoid the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that Simo Drljaca addressed the people after the massacre that occurred in Room 3 in Keraterm. You testified that he said something to the effect that this should not have happened. Do you know who it was that he was addressing? Was he talking to the guards or the detainees?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I don't think I'm able to tell you who exactly it was he was addressing. He was standing in the middle of a group of people, that is, the people who were there. And the message was passed on us to detainees that what happened was the result of a mistake and that in the future, we would be better protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One more point from today's testimony, on page 56, you told us who accompanied Simo Drljaca, and you mentioned that there was a man there whose one arm was missing.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a man there who had one arm missing from elbow down. And he was wearing a white coat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you think he was a doctor?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was because of this coat that he had that I thought he was a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I've asked you this only in order to clarify a point in the transcript because the record reflects that there was a man without one hand, and another man. But actually, we're talking about one and the same person. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When meetings were held in Kozarac, the meetings which were attended by Mr. Medunjanin and his collaborators, when he informed you, the residents of Kozarac, on the prevailing situation in the Prijedor Municipality, who organised, who convened these meetings if you know?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Usually a local resident would inform us that there would be a meeting and where the venue would be, and that there would be some new pieces of information. But mostly, as I say, it was the local residents who would inform us about such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it a unanimous decision, the decision not to sign the oath of loyalty to Serb authorities, or was there any outvoting? How was the decision not to sign the oath of loyalty reached?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: At the meetings that I attended, the decision was made unanimously but the Kozarac residents. They decided that the oath of loyalty should not be signed. However, they also stated that as far as we were concerned, the Prijedor authorities could be sure that we would not attack anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many days after the takeover the first such meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, a couple of days later perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there ever -- were there ever any incidents at your checkpoint, at the point overlooking the village of Balte, prior to the 24th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that a large number of people from Balte were mobilised and that they were not in their village at the time but deployed at the front line?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever establish any contact with the population of Balte during these guard shifts?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a shop not far from Balte. I think that people from Balte came to this shop from time to time, and we would occasionally have a chat. I think that this happened even after the takeover in Prijedor. I mean, these people were familiar to us. We knew them very well. They were our neighbours, after all. Some of them even paid us a visit in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Seven days prior to the outbreak of fighting in Kozarac, at the Prijedor/Banja Luka Road, at at least two locations on this main road in the village of Kozarusa and the village of Jakupovici, there were both Serb and Bosniak barricades, roadblocks, that is?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I don't think we can talk about roadblocks. As far as our side is concerned, those were just regular guards as we had in Kozarac. I mean, those were not machine-gun nests surrounded by sandbags. It was just a group of people who were there just in case of an attack, in order to ensure normal traffic on that road including the population and the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. vehicles so that the traffic would function normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony today that the traffic was normal on that road at that time?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: At the time, seven days before the attack, no. Up until that time, yes. However, when the presence of the guards was intensified, no, despite the fact that there were no physical barricades on the road. This was practically a response to the setting up of a checkpoint in Orlovci, because as a result of that, we were not able to travel to Prijedor. We were not able to travel to Omarska, so we knew that something was brewing, that something would soon happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of a request issued by the Banja Luka command concerning a passage of a military convoy on the 24th of May, 1992, when the conflict in Kozarac broke out?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you must be aware of the fact that on that day, there was a convoy of military vehicles moving from the direction of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard when Kapetan Cirkin was being briefed by a commander from the local checkpoint there, that is, the checkpoint in Jakupovici, who was telling him that a military convoy was approaching?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also heard when Kapetan Cirkin issued commands to the person who had called him from that checkpoint, that is, when he told him that he shall let the tanks come close to him, close enough so that he could destroy them with a hand-held rocket launcher, with a Zolja?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the convoy did not consist only of tanks, but also of infantry troops. It was not an ordinary military convoy moving along a road. It was a classical military attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at least one of the tanks was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that's what I heard subsequently that one was destroyed, and that one was put out of order. Whether this information is accurate, I don't know. I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, it is clear from this command issued by Kapetan Cirkin that he knew that the people manning the checkpoint in Jakupovici had Zoljas at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was probably the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time of the negotiations with the Serb side, you said that the decisions that were reached would be transmitted by telephone.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question. What do you mean by "telephone"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is whether the telephone communication was possible at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I don't think that the telephone lines were operating after the takeover. It's possible that there was telephone communication between the police station in Kozarac and the police station in Prijedor, so that was probably the channel that was used for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of radio station did you have at your guard post?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: We had this old-fashioned type of police radio station which was improved, but later it stopped functioning because we didn't have batteries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But they were working on the day of the attack because Kapetan Cirkin was able to use them to communicate with the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about your radio station, was it built in in your vehicle, or was it a portable hand-held radio station?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No, it was just a small portable hand-held radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the majority of the Kozarac population believe that the situation would be peacefully solved?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe they did. I think that at the time the majority of the Kozarac residents sincerely wished for a peaceful solution to be found in order for the conflict to be avoided. I don't think that -- I think that more than 90 per cent of us believed that there would not be any kind of conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, the fact remains that at the same time, the population was being armed and that the conditions put out by Serb authorities were not accepted, including the signing of an oath of loyalty?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of any arming of the population. As to accepting the conditions of Serb authorities, I think that what local people considered to be their government were people who had been legally elected at the elections, those who had taken power by force, we didn't consider them as "legal" authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is somewhat difficult to talk about legality and legal authorities at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I'm not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because then we would have to consider the issue of mobilisation, and we would have to consider those who were not responding to mobilisation as violating the legal request.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Well, there were people -- I think that the majority of people, Croats and Bosniaks from Bosnia and Herzegovina, we did not want to go to fight war in Croatia. I think that at least as far as I am concerned, if I had been mobilised to go to Croatia and to fight Croats there, I don't think I would have responded to the mobilisation call. We, the people of Kozarac, never attacked anyone. Even today, if you go to the area of Kozarac, you can see for yourself that not a single Serb house had been attacked. We never attacked any Serb villages. I wanted to remain at home. I wanted to live peacefully, and I was naive enough to have moved into my family house 20 days before the outbreak of the conflict. I really believed in peace. I wanted to live there with my family. Those were my thoughts at the time. But it seems that I was naive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You may have been naive, but did you notice that other people were sending their families away?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the people in Kozarac, that they sent away their families from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that those people who had means to do that did send their families away. I didn't do that. I didn't feel the need to go and leave my home. I didn't think it was necessary for me to protect myself in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did anyone convey to you the exact request of the Serb authorities from the population of Kozarac immediately prior to the attack? And if so, what was it that was conveyed to us? What was the request made of the population of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: What I learned before the attack was that they wanted Becir Medunjanin and two other residents of Kozarac, the representative of the local religious community, and one other person to come to the checkpoint in Orlovci to talk to Radmilo Zeljaja. However, they kept repeating their request that the people of Kozarac should sign an oath of loyalty and turn in their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the majority of the negotiations were held with Radmilo Zeljaja?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: That's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether any minutes of that meeting were kept?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No, I was not present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When the delegation returned from the last round of talks, and after they had explained to the people what the situation was, did people as a result of that become even more resolute in their intention to defend Kozarac, or whether they were inclined to meet the requests of Radmilo Zeljaja?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Well, they still -- they still maintained their position, that is, that they would not attack anyone, but also that likewise they did not want to sign any oath of loyalty or turn in the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me now go back to the checkpoints in Kozarusa and Jakupovici. You heard over the radio set that hand-to-hand fighting had started at these two checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I believe that it happened at the Jakupovici checkpoint, that the convoy started moving and the people manning the checkpoint had no choice and started retreating towards Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Towards the centre of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the checkpoint or the guard post where you were, you ordered your people to open fire two by two so that it would look that they had more ammunition than they, in fact, did?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the people in Jakupovici -- at the Jakupovici told us that they didn't have enough time to pull out all the women and children, that the attack was coming from the direction of the village of Balte, and that was the reason why we opened fire. But we didn't have enough ammunition. We thought that if we opened fire, the attack would decrease in its intensity and that it would give enough time to the people of Jakupovici to pull out their women and children out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the distance between Jakupovici and the centre of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: The distance between Jakupovici and the centre of Kozarac is perhaps 5 or 6 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The fact is, therefore, that the fighting that you started did, in fact, keep the Serbs at bay and that it took them two days to reach the centre of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. We did open fire, but fighting occurred in Jakupovici as well, that is, on the road, the Prijedor/Banja Luka Road. And the distance between that and the centre of Kozarac is 4 or 5 -- 3 to 4 kilometres, that is, from Kozarac and the road where the fighting took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May I be permitted --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt my friend at this stage, but the question reads: "The fact is, therefore, that the fighting that you started did..." There was no such position taken by the witness, just for the record, Your Honour. That's incorrectly stated by the learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to -- I wanted to ask the witness about the fighting that he and his men joined in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The witness never said or stated that he started the fighting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It may have been the interpreter's mistake, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for your intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] And I want to thank the interpreters for helping me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know who issued the order for the guard shifts to last 24 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: When the takeover in Prijedor took place, we knew that something was going on and the decision was made that there should be a round-the-clock guard duty. We wanted to prevent any incident from occurring in the town of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that moment, was the number of guard posts increased?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Probably, yes. Where we were, the village was inhabited, and the inhabitants also watched the outer perimeter of the village just in case someone was to be prevented from penetrating the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were these guard posts positioned at regular intervals along the whole perimeter of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: We didn't have the sufficient number of people to have guard posts proper. Those were patrols of two or three persons, just surveying the situation to keep anything bad from happening. That's mostly how this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, immediately before the attack at your guard post, at your own guard post, there were 50 people. Right?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: 50 people? If you count the inhabitants who were also there, then perhaps even more, but that was an inhabited village, and we who actually stood guard duty, we were perhaps about 10 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that later. You said at one point that you only took orders from Becir Medunjanin, and Osme, the police chief.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: We obtained information from them on the current situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there anyone in the Kozarac area who was in terms of hierarchy above these two men?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I think people mostly talked to Becir or Besim Alic or to Cirkin concerning police matters because those were the people who represented the people at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something else concerning the radio sets. How often did you use radio connections to send reports about the situation on the ground, and who did you send these reports to?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: We never sent any reports of the kind. The radio sets were used for us to obtain new information should there be any new developments, of course. We were only receiving instructions to the effect that we should never open fire on anyone or return fire. It mostly came down to just having some sort of a communications system so we could be informed about any new possible developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember a situation you described at one point, Zeljaja requested that Medunjanin, Besim Alic, who was president of the citizens club in Kozarac, and other two citizens from Kozarac as well as a Muslim religious leader should come to the Orlovci checkpoint for further negotiations to reach some sort of an agreement?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've talked about this already. That was the last attempt to come to an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Mr. Medunjanin replied?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: He replied that the people of Kozarac did not want to sign any oath of loyalty, but that both he and the people of Kozarac could offer guarantees, sure guarantees, to the people in Prijedor that we would not carry out any attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Medunjanin try to organise another meeting after this?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I think he simply informed the citizens about what happened at the meeting, and that's how it ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know the checkpoints in Jakupovici and Kozarusa, there was a mine field surrounding those checkpoints? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No, I've never heard of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to review a completely different area now. Can you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. please try to think back and recall the moment when you were released from Trnopolje on the 1st of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On that occasion were any conditions imposed on you that you should sign over your property to the Autonomous Region of Krajina or Republika Srpska or was there no talk of that at all in fact?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I think the signing of the documents we were given, first you had to file a request for emigration, and then you had to sign over your property. I think that was part of the forms, the documents, we were given. And then later on we received a decision stating that our emigration from the Serbian Krajina was approved. Signing the document was a condition for us to leave -- in order to leave the camp. I had nothing to sign over at that moment anyway, because all of my property had been razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Keraterm case, page 1601, when you were questioned by Mr. Ryneveld, I'll read this in English so you get a proper translation. The question is: [In English] "Was there any mention made of your property and what would happen to it?" Your answer was: "No, nobody raised that."

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: It's quite possible that that was indeed what I replied. The question really wasn't raised, but the condition to leave the camp was to sign over your property. Had I done this under any normal conditions, of course, I would never had chosen to leave my own country and my home after so many years. I was compelled to file a request for emigration from the Serbian Krajina. And following that, I was not able to return to my home for the next ten years. I'm not sure that anyone in the right state of mind and under normal conditions would do a thing like that, file a motion like that with some local authorities and then go away and leave for somewhere, leaving their home behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I feel I fully understand how you feel.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No, you don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because I shared your situation. I was in the same situation as you. However, are you today positive that you signed this document signing over your property, or are you not positive?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: No, I signed no direct statement signing over my property to anyone else, but I did sign a request for emigration. And I was sent a decision that a certain committee in Prijedor Municipality approves my emigration, and that I could emigrate of my own free will. But we all know that this was not my will. I was compelled to emigrate; otherwise, I would not have been able to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I accept this, and that's not what I'm asking you. I mean, that you were compelled to file a request to emigrate. My question was: Are you sure that you actually signed your property over to someone else or renounced on your property?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know this, but I know that if I go back to Prijedor Municipality today, I have to file a request for my property to be given back to me because it was taken away from me. I can't go back to my home until I get a permission from the authorities in Prijedor to have my property back, which means that it was taken away from me at some point. The only thing that still remains is the land.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you will agree that this is the legal frame that is valid both in the Bosnian federation and in Republika Srpska nowadays, and that this is valid no matter whether someone has renounced their property or not?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the situation concerning laws in Bosnia and Herzegovina nowadays, but I know that when I go there to have something which is mine back, as far as I am familiar with international law, private property is inalienable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In our country, there are lots of things that are not normal or common in the rest of the world.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we should try and struggle to change these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I fully agree with you, but we must go back to the hearing at hand. In your statement of the 28th of February, 1995, to the investigators of the Tribunal, you contend that you as well as many other inmates were in possession of an ID in the Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I did, and I still am in possession of my old Bosnian ID today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could Defence counsel please be so kind and come back to our formal good habit to quote the page and the paragraph. It facilitates really to come back to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I have B/C/S. It's page 4, paragraph 1. But I don't have an English version at all. In English, the paragraph should start: "As far as I remember, at the end of July..." Something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The statement of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 1995, yes. That's the only question I have from this statement, so that's why I didn't want to bother you with the photocopying and...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the following: The army arriving in the Prijedor area from the beginning of 1992. Did all that army stay in Prijedor, or were most of those units just passing through Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Some of the units were just passing through. The units staying there, I don't know. But this unit stayed -- passed through Kozarac and was stationed for a long time near Mrakovica. Some other units may have been stationed close to Prijedor, but convoys were passing to and through every day. So I wasn't sure about the direction of each and every convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this also partly due to the withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: I think so, because that's what we were told, that the JNA was withdrawing from Croatia and taking most -- taking a large share of the units over into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I must ask you something that you have been asked before by my colleague Greaves in the Keraterm trial. I will read part of your testimony and I will ask you whether you remember stating that. It's about the 27th of May when most of the people of Kozarac were surrendering to the Serb forces. And you decided to head towards Kozara with your own group and link up with Kapetan Cirkin. This is on page 7, English version, the statement of 1994, paragraph 4. I'd like to quote a piece from the middle of the paragraph. You go on to say: "We passed the road, Kozarac/Mrakovica, in an attempt to link up with Kapetan Cirkin and Medunjanin. As we passed the road at Zeciji Kamen, there was a Serbian checkpoint. A fight then ensued, and about 120 of the persons from our group were arrested. I believe that some of those arrested were killed immediately, and that others were transferred to Omarska." Do you remember having stated that?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this true?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We came under fire, and about 120 people were arrested. I think first they were taken to Benkovac, and then later on to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The following paragraph, just after this sentence, you say: "The rest of us escaped but stayed in the area. We eventually found Kapetan Cirkin and Medunjanin. They were with a group of about 750 people. Some among this group were women. Some of them wanted to attempt to cross over into Croatia, and others wanted to mount a new attack. We opted for a new attack. We split up into three groups with about 250 people each. The group I joined attacked Kozarac from Brdjani." So my question is: How many people really took part in this new attempt to liberate or conquer Kozarac, depending on which side you're looking from?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: The group with Becir Medunjanin and Cirkin consisted of about 750 people. Some wanted to go to Croatia, but others wanted to return to Kozarac. I would not call this an attack. There was no need for me to attack my own town. On the other side, there were our own women and children who had been taken away. The only thing we could try was to return to our homes in Kozarac. I think there were people who tried to return, but they were the minority, and no one had control or knew exactly how many people were taking part. But then people tried to get into the town. And when tanks started firing again, as well as the artillery, the only thing they could do was retreat again towards Mount Kozara.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You described the battle in the next paragraph. I quote: "A fight broke out between the two groups, but when they started attacking with the tank, we withdrew to the area of Kozaracki Kamen. I could hear sounds of fighting near the centre of Kozarac, and I realised that the other two groups had been successful in their attempt to break through to the centre. I later found out that they had been outnumbered by the enemy and that they had also withdrawn from the village." Did you later learn whether these two groups really managed to reach the centre of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: JUSUF ARIFAGIC
utterances.text: On their way to Kozarac, near Kozarac, near the centre of Kozarac, they came across Serb troops who opened fire, and then several young men were killed, and they withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honour, I think that I have another half an hour at least with this witness. So should I proceed or...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, I think it's appropriate to restart tomorrow; also from the side of the Judges, there are some questions remaining. And let's proceed with the cross-examination tomorrow. The OTP stands up. There must be a --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I had an oral motion, a very brief one, if I could make it, unrelated to the witness. There is a report being prepared, there's a draft -- should be available this afternoon, regarding the exhumations that were performed by both the ICTY and the Bosnians in the area that were concerning victims from Prijedor. The report names many of our witnesses, so for that reason I'm asking permission from the Trial Chamber to file that confidentially. It's to the Defence, but not publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt agreed. And I would be more than happy to hear my second language as soon as possible on a video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's available for both parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it formally tendered as evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm not -- we weren't going to do that. I can review it again and see. To be honest, I watched it a very long time ago, and haven't watched it recently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's come back to this tomorrow. Anything else in preparation for tomorrow? What can we expect in case we can conclude the cross-examination during the morning session?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We don't have any witnesses from abroad or experts ready. We have the video that was provided by Witness Sivac which is about 10 or 15 minutes - the transcript is prepared - we could play that. And Mr. Inayat would be available also, if that's an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you be prepared to cross-examine? I asked you several times during the last month, and now we should take the occasion when you are here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We anticipate to be prepared, Your Honour. So it all depends on what his direct examination is. But we look forward to seeing Mr. Inayat again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for being prepared. And first of all, I have to thank our witness of today for giving us the information and for being prepared to give additional information tomorrow. Thank you for this. You're excused for today. The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 9.30, without any doubt. 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
